Session-by-session record of hands-on work with the robots, newest
first — one dated entry per session, written so both an advisor and a
non-engineer can follow it. The technical reference behind these
entries is the [platform notes](platform-notes.qmd); formal weekly
summaries live in the [weekly updates](../../updates/index.qmd).

## 2026-08-27 — Day 1 with the robot

### The goal

Before a robot can learn anything, my laptop and the robot have to
talk to each other. Today's job was to establish that conversation:
hear everything the robot senses, and prove my laptop can tell the
robot what to do — the two pipes that all the thesis work will flow
through.

### What happened

**Getting connected took detective work.** The robot speaks over the
lab's Wi-Fi, but my laptop runs its robot software inside a Linux
compartment (WSL), and Windows was silently guarding that compartment's
door: security rules dropped the robot's replies before they arrived.
Everything *looked* configured correctly and nothing worked — until we
found the right firewall gate to open. This is now fixed permanently;
the laptop connects on its own from here on.

**Then the robot came through loud and clear.** We catalogued
everything it broadcasts — 49 data channels — and watched its joint
angles stream live in a terminal while I drove the arm with the
teleoperation tablet.

**We caught the tablet's commands mid-flight.** While I teleoperated,
my laptop recorded over a thousand of the exact command messages the
tablet sends the arm. This matters because a learned policy will speak
through this same channel — now we know its precise format: six speed
values (move/turn in each direction) plus one gripper number. Seven
numbers, a hundred times a second. That is the language the robot is
commanded in.

**And the finale: my laptop moved the arm.** A two-second command
stream sent from my keyboard raised the arm three centimetres,
smoothly, and it stopped by itself — with a hand on the emergency stop
the whole time. External control: proven.

### The numbers that shape what comes next

| Measurement | Value | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Joint angle updates | ~10 per second | matches the planned learning rate |
| Camera (on the robot) | 15 images/sec, full HD | healthy at the source |
| Camera (over Wi-Fi) | only ~3.4 images/sec arrive | Wi-Fi can't carry raw video → **demonstrations must be recorded on the robot's own computer**, exactly as planned |
| Tablet command rate | ~119 messages/sec | the arm wants 100/sec — confirmed feasible |
| Clock difference laptop ↔ robot | ~1 second | harmless for recording (one clock does it all); must be synchronized before live deployment |

### Bottom line

Both pipes work: robot → laptop (all senses readable) and laptop →
robot (commands obeyed). The day-1 checklist closed with every box
ticked, and the next step is the recording pipeline: capturing human
demonstrations on the robot's own computer in the format the learning
software expects.
